The craze for Japanese art in France and the rest of the West in the late 1800s. After Japan opened its ports in the 1850s, Japanese prints, fans and ceramics reached Europe, and Japan's displays at the Paris Exposition of 1867 drew large crowds. The French critic Philippe Burty coined the word japonisme in 1872.

Woodblock prints of the ukiyo-e school, by artists such as Hokusai and Hiroshige, were cheap in Japan and a revelation in Paris. Their flat colours, bold outlines, empty space and odd viewpoints, cut off at the edges, showed a way out of academic painting.

  • Claude Monet collected prints and built a Japanese bridge over his water lily pond at Giverny.
  • Vincent van Gogh copied prints by Hiroshige in oil.
  • Whistler, Degas and Toulouse-Lautrec borrowed their way of framing a scene.

The influence runs through Impressionism, poster art and Art Nouveau, and The Great Wave became one of the best known images in the West.
